title: The Fifteen Papers
dek: Every AI agent you can build today is a stack of about fifteen ideas, published between 2017 and 2025. This is the list: what each one did, in one line, what it is responsible for now, and the link to the paper itself. Nothing is here for being famous. It is here because it is in your stack.
summary: The fifteen research papers, 2017 to 2025, that a working AI agent is built out of: one line each, the impact in keywords, and the link.
hand: If it isn't in your stack

blocks.html: You have heard the names. Someone on a podcast says “since the Chinchilla paper” and everyone nods. A repo README cites ReAct. A model card mentions DPO. You could go and read them all. You will not, and you should not: most papers since 2017 are increments on a handful of others. This is the handful.

The rule for making the list was narrow on purpose. A paper is here if the agent you can build this afternoon would not work, or would not exist, without it. Famous is not enough. Clever is not enough. It has to be load-bearing in your stack today. That gives fifteen, and a second tier that nearly made it, at the end.

Between 2017 and 2025 the field did about seven things, roughly in order. It found a better building block (the Transformer). It learnt to pre-train that block once and reuse it (BERT). It worked out that making it bigger pays predictably (scaling laws, GPT-3, Chinchilla). It taught the model to take instructions instead of just continuing text (InstructGPT). It got the model to reason and to act in plain text (chain-of-thought, ReAct). It gave the weights away (LoRA, LLaMA, latent diffusion, DPO). And finally it made reasoning itself something you train rather than prompt (test-time compute, DeepSeek-R1). Everything else is plumbing on those seven.
Take one boring thing an agent does. You ask it why last night’s build failed. It reads the log, runs a command, reads the output, and tells you. Every part of that one turn has a paper behind it.

blocks.caption: One agent turn. The model is the Transformer block, trained to the scaling recipes and then tuned to follow instructions. Chain-of-thought lets it think in text; ReAct lets that text ask for a tool; the tool’s output comes back in as context, through the same door retrieval uses. The loop runs until the model writes an answer instead of a request.

blocks.html: Grouped by what they changed, not strictly by year. The middle column is what the paper did, in one breath. The last column is what it is responsible for in your stack today. Every link goes to the paper itself, on arXiv, not to a summary of it.

head: Year
Paper
What it did
Now responsible for
rows: The block, then the scale
Attention Is All You Need · Vaswani et al., Google
Threw out recurrence. Every token attends to every other token at once, so training parallelises across GPUs instead of crawling along the sequence.
Transformer · every LLM since · GPU-scale training
BERT · Devlin et al., Google
Pre-train once on raw text, fine-tune cheaply per task. Made download a pre-trained model the default workflow.
pre-train / fine-tune · embeddings · search ranking · the Hugging Face era
Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models · Kaplan et al., OpenAI
Loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute. Bigger stopped being a gamble and became a budget line.
the case for the spend · compute planning · “just scale it”
Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3) · Brown et al., OpenAI
175 billion parameters. A new task from a few examples in the prompt, no fine-tuning. Prompting became programming.
in-context learning · prompt engineering · the API business model
Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla) · Hoffmann et al., DeepMind
Most models were under-trained. For a fixed budget, use a smaller model and far more tokens; roughly twenty tokens per parameter.
tokens over parameters · 7B–70B models · why a local model is usable
Steering it
Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (InstructGPT) · Ouyang et al., OpenAI
The RLHF recipe: demonstrations, then a reward model from human rankings, then optimise against it. A 1.3B model tuned this way was preferred over the 175B original. ChatGPT is this, applied.
RLHF · the “assistant” · ChatGPT
Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning · Wei et al., Google
Ask for the intermediate steps and reasoning accuracy jumps, but only at scale (around 100B parameters at the time). Reasoning became something a model does in text.
“think step by step” · reasoning traces · the seed of o1 and R1
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) · Rafailov et al., Stanford
Same preference alignment as RLHF with no reward model and no RL loop: a simple loss over pairs of answers. Alignment became something one person with one GPU can do.
RLHF without RL · every open fine-tune · Zephyr, Llama 3 post-training
Acting
Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP (RAG) · Lewis et al., Facebook AI
Bolt a retriever onto a generator so the answer comes from fetched documents rather than from memory. Named the pattern.
“chat with your docs” · vector databases · grounding · citations
ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models · Yao et al., Princeton and Google
Interleave a thought, an action (a tool call) and the observation that comes back, in one text loop. That loop is the agent.
the agent loop · tool use · LangChain agents · Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw
Open weights
LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models · Hu et al., Microsoft
Freeze the model, train two small low-rank matrices per layer. About 10,000× fewer trainable parameters and no extra inference latency.
cheap fine-tuning · adapters · QLoRA · every community fine-tune
High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models · Rombach et al., LMU Munich and Runway
Run diffusion in a compressed latent space instead of on pixels, so image generation fits a consumer GPU. Shipped as Stable Diffusion in August 2022.
Stable Diffusion · open image generation · ControlNet · image LoRAs
LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models · Touvron et al., Meta
A 13B model trained Chinchilla-style on public data beat GPT-3. The weights got out within a week and the local-model ecosystem appeared in a fortnight.
open weights · llama.cpp · Ollama · the whole local stack
Reasoning that is trained, not prompted
Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters · Snell et al., Berkeley and DeepMind

Spend more compute at inference (more samples, a verifier, revision) and a small model can beat one 14× larger on the same budget. Named the second scaling axis; OpenAI’s o1 shipped five weeks later with a blog post, not a paper.
test-time compute · thinking budgets · “reasoning effort”
DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning · DeepSeek-AI
Pure RL with checkable rewards on a base model, no reasoning examples, and long chain-of-thought appeared on its own (R1-Zero). The recipe was published, with MIT-licensed weights.
RL with verifiable rewards · GRPO · open reasoning models · the January 2025 market shock

blocks.title: Where these get quoted wrong
blocks.label: Check before you repeat it
blocks.html:
Chinchilla’s twenty tokens per parameter is the optimum for training compute. If you will serve the model a billion times, inference dominates and you overtrain on purpose: Llama 3 8B was trained on over 15 trillion tokens, nearer 1,900 per parameter.

Chain-of-thought in the 2022 paper only helped very large models; on small ones it made answers worse. Today’s small models reason because R1-style training put it in the weights, not because you typed “think step by step”.

RAG the paper trained the retriever and the generator together. RAG the product is usually “paste the top five chunks into the prompt”. Useful, but not what the paper measured.

ReAct’s numbers came from a 540B PaLM on question-answering and text-game benchmarks. The benchmarks did not matter. The one idea that did: the tool’s output goes back into the context, so the next thought can see it.

The 2020 scaling-law constants were overturned by Chinchilla two years later. The shape held; the numbers did not. Quote the shape.

These are real and worth your time; they just are not load-bearing for a working agent in the way the fifteen are. Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences (2017) is the root RLHF grew from. GPT-2 (2019) argued that one language model does many tasks, and started the staged-release habit. ViT (2020) and CLIP (2021) took the Transformer into images and put text and images in one space; CLIP is what most image generators are steered by. FlashAttention (2022) is why long context is affordable at all. Constitutional AI (2022) replaced human harmlessness labels with AI feedback against a written set of rules. Toolformer (2023) had the model teach itself when to call an API. Let’s Verify Step by Step (2023) rewarded each reasoning step rather than the final answer. The GPT-4 Technical Report (2023) is notable for what it withheld: the moment frontier labs stopped publishing architecture. Generative Agents (2023) gave agents memory and reflection. SWE-bench (2023) is the exam coding agents are graded on. Mamba (2023) is the credible non-Transformer. Mixtral (2024) and DeepSeek-V3 (2024) made mixture-of-experts the open default. s1 (2025) reproduced test-time scaling with a thousand examples and a budget on the word “wait”.

Nothing from 2026 is on the list. Not because nothing happened: DeepSeek-V4 (April 2026) put a million-token context in open weights, and hybrid state-space models are shipping from several labs. “Changed the most” needs about a year to become visible. The list is revised when something earns a place; the stamp below says when it was last checked.

blocks.title: If you only read three
blocks.label: Twenty minutes each
blocks.html:
Abstract, figure 1, the ablation table. Skip the related work.

Attention Is All You Need, section 3 and figure 1. The block. Once you can draw it, every model card makes sense.

InstructGPT, figure 2 and section 3.5. The three-step recipe every assistant you have ever talked to was made with.

ReAct, section 2 and one full trajectory from the appendix. That trajectory is what your agent framework is doing under the logs.

blocks.text: The whole thing in three sentences

blocks.html: A Transformer trained at scale is the engine. Instruction tuning made it take orders, chain-of-thought made it think in text, and ReAct made that text able to act. Open weights and cheap fine-tuning put the whole thing on your machine, and RL on checkable rewards is now teaching it to think better without being told how.
